questionText: What is a critical section?
options: Every instruction in a private local calculation
Any function longer than one page
Only a program's final return statement
Code accessing shared state that needs coordinated access
explanation: Critical sections protect shared operations whose overlapping execution could violate an invariant.

questionText: What is the typical purpose of a mutex?
options: Translate virtual addresses
Allow one owner at a time into a protected section
Create a new process every time it locks
Store file data permanently
explanation: A mutex provides mutual exclusion around shared resources or state.

questionText: What does it mean for an operation to be atomic relative to other participating operations?
options: It appears indivisible to them
It needs no CPU instructions
It always takes one nanosecond
It automatically writes to disk
explanation: Atomicity is an indivisibility guarantee, not a claim about duration or persistence.

questionText: What does a thread do while waiting on a simple spinlock?
options: Repeatedly checks or attempts the lock
Deletes the protected object
Reboots the processor
Necessarily sleeps in the kernel
explanation: A spinlock uses active waiting; this can be appropriate for very short waits in suitable contexts.

questionText: What is a condition variable mainly used for?
options: Replacing a thread's stack
Waiting until shared state may satisfy a predicate
Automatically remembering an unlimited signal count
Storing the protected data itself
explanation: Condition variables coordinate waiting for state changes; the predicate is stored in shared state and checked under a lock.

questionText: What does a barrier synchronization point require?
options: Participating threads reach a common phase boundary before proceeding
All processes have the same PID
Every thread terminate immediately
Only the first thread may ever continue
explanation: A barrier coordinates phases of a parallel computation so required participants finish one phase before the next.

questionText: A resource pool has 6 identical available units. What initial counting-semaphore value represents this?
explanation: A counting semaphore can represent available units, so an entirely free six-unit pool starts at six.

questionText: In a queue, what is the producer's role?
options: Collect process exit status
Translate virtual addresses
Choose the next disk cylinder
Add items for a consumer to remove
explanation: Producers generate queued work or data; consumers take it for processing.

questionText: Why can a reader-writer lock permit several readers together?
options: Multiple readers always need exclusive mutation rights
Readers have no CPU registers
Read-only participants do not modify the protected state
Readers automatically receive private copies of every file
explanation: Concurrent reads can coexist, while a writer requires exclusion from conflicting accesses.

questionText: Which variable is least likely to need inter-thread locking by itself?
options: A mutable global linked list
A shared bank balance
A stack-local counter whose address never escapes its thread
A shared global queue head
explanation: State accessed by only one thread does not create an inter-thread conflict.

questionText: Why should code release a mutex after finishing the protected work?
options: Unlocking makes all prior calculations disappear
Other waiting threads need access to the resource
It changes the process's PID
A mutex can be used only once
explanation: Retaining ownership blocks other participants and can prevent progress.

questionText: What resource does busy waiting primarily consume while no useful work completes?
options: CPU time
Printer paper
Extra disk cylinders
Additional user accounts
explanation: A spinning waiter executes instructions instead of doing useful application work or sleeping.

questionText: Can threads on a single CPU still have concurrency bugs?
options: Yes; interleaving at preemption points can expose shared-state races
No; races require two physical CPUs
Only if the filesystem is full
No; every source statement is atomic
explanation: Concurrency includes interleaved execution, so shared compound operations can race even without simultaneous CPU execution.

questionText: What does a bounded-waiting guarantee limit?
options: The number of arithmetic operations in the OS
The maximum disk file name length
The total size of all program files
How long or how many entries others can make before a requester gets access
explanation: Bounded waiting addresses starvation by limiting indefinite postponement under the stated algorithm's assumptions.

questionText: Two threads each read a shared counter as 0, then each writes its read value plus 1. What final value can result?
options: 2 only
Minus 1
explanation: Both compute 1 from the same old value; the second store overwrites the first increment.

questionText: Why does a normal x++ on shared memory generally need more reasoning than an atomic increment?
options: It is necessarily a system call
It cannot modify memory
It may consist of separate load, compute and store operations
It always holds a mutex automatically
explanation: Interleaving separate steps can lose updates; an appropriate atomic operation gives a single indivisible modification.

questionText: Why should a condition wait normally appear in a while loop checking its predicate?
options: Every wakeup permanently grants resource ownership
The mutex must never be reacquired
Condition variables store the predicate automatically
Wakeup does not guarantee the predicate is true when the thread resumes
explanation: Spurious wakeups and other threads consuming the condition require rechecking protected state.

questionText: Why must a condition wait atomically release its mutex and begin waiting?
options: To copy the whole heap to disk
To guarantee the process will never be scheduled again
To avoid a notification being lost between checking and sleeping
To remove the need for shared predicates
explanation: Atomic release-and-wait closes the race where a signal occurs after the predicate check but before the waiter is registered.

questionText: A semaphore is posted before a thread waits, with no intervening wait. How does this differ from a bare condition signal with no waiters?
options: Both necessarily retain one message payload
The condition signal permanently locks a mutex
The semaphore loses all counts automatically
The semaphore retains a permit; the condition signal need not be retained
explanation: Semaphores maintain counts, whereas condition variables notify existing waiters about state stored elsewhere.

questionText: What is a common tradeoff of fine-grained locking?
options: Elimination of all shared mutable state
Guaranteed absence of deadlock
More parallelism but greater lock-management complexity
No need to define lock order
explanation: More independent locks reduce unnecessary exclusion but complicate reasoning about interactions and ordering.

questionText: Why is a blocking mutex often preferable to spinning during a long wait on a single CPU?
options: Blocking erases the protected data
Spinning creates more CPU cores
The owner cannot run unless the waiter spins
The waiter can yield CPU time to useful work
explanation: Active waiting can waste the CPU the owner or other work needs to make progress.

questionText: What problem can a reader-preference policy cause if readers continually arrive?
options: Writer starvation
Writers gain infinite priority
Files become physically fragmented
Every reader is guaranteed to deadlock
explanation: New readers can repeatedly delay a waiting writer unless the policy bounds that bypass.

questionText: Under Mesa-style condition signaling, what does a signaled thread generally do?
options: Take permanent ownership of every monitor
Skip rechecking the shared condition
Become eligible to run and later reacquire the monitor lock
Run immediately while bypassing the lock
explanation: The signaler can continue; the waiter competes to reacquire the lock and must recheck its predicate.

questionText: Why can releasing and acquiring the same correctly used mutex matter beyond exclusion?
options: It establishes ordering and visibility guarantees for protected writes
It makes all data persistent on disk
It invalidates every private stack
It automatically repairs unprotected data races elsewhere
explanation: Synchronization primitives provide specified memory-order relationships, not merely scheduling decisions.

questionText: Why is blocking on slow network I/O while holding a broad mutex often undesirable?
options: Network I/O cannot block
A mutex guarantees the remote peer responds instantly
Holding the lock increases network bandwidth by definition
It unnecessarily delays unrelated threads needing that lock
explanation: Long waits enlarge the critical section and can serialize otherwise independent operations.

questionText: A buffer has capacity 8 and currently holds 3 items. With conventional empty/full semaphores, what are their counts when no operations are in flight?
options: empty=3, full=5
empty=8, full=3
empty=5, full=3
empty=0, full=8
explanation: Free slots equal capacity minus occupied slots: 8-3=5; three items are available to consume.

questionText: Four workers must all finish phase 1 before any starts phase 2. Which primitive directly expresses this requirement?
options: An unlocked integer alone
A four-participant barrier
A file-name lookup
A private thread-local flag in each thread
explanation: A barrier coordinates completion across participants rather than protecting one shared object at a time.

questionText: A compare-and-swap expects 7 but sees 9. Under standard semantics, what happens to the target value?
options: The process necessarily exits
It becomes zero
It remains 9 and the comparison fails
It becomes 7 unconditionally
explanation: CAS changes the target only when its current value equals the expected value.

questionText: Two cores repeatedly modify different counters on the same cache line. What can hurt performance?
options: The absence of any cache-line transfers
Cache-coherence traffic despite logically independent data
Automatic filesystem corruption
A guaranteed lost update between different addresses
explanation: Coherence operates at cache-line granularity, so unrelated mutable variables can interfere through placement.

questionText: A counting semaphore starts at 4. Three successful waits occur, then two posts, with no other operations. What count remains?
explanation: The available-permit count becomes 4-3+2=3; no wait needed to block in this sequence.

questionText: Why can two individually thread-safe calls still need a surrounding lock when combined?
options: An invariant may depend on the pair being indivisible
Each call automatically reserves future calls
Thread-safe means every possible sequence is atomic
Locks cannot span two function calls
explanation: Thread safety of individual operations does not make a multi-step check-then-act sequence atomic.

questionText: Two threads repeatedly back off and retry to accommodate each other but never complete. What is this called?
options: Successful mutual exclusion
Livelock
Static linking
Page replacement
explanation: Livelock involves continuing activity without useful progress, unlike threads simply blocked without activity.

questionText: When is it valid to protect one shared object with two unrelated mutexes?
options: Always on a multicore processor
Only when the mutex names have equal length
Only if another design guarantee prevents conflicting access; unrelated locks alone do not protect it
Always, because any mutex protects all memory
explanation: Participants must follow a common synchronization protocol; different independent locks do not exclude one another.

questionText: Why is the predicate usually changed while holding the same mutex used by condition waiters?
options: To prevent any future wakeups
To turn the condition variable into a file
To keep predicate checks and updates in one coherent synchronization protocol
To remove the need for loops
explanation: Shared locking coordinates the state transition with the waiter's check and atomic wait operation.

questionText: What does lock contention mean?
options: A process has no executable image
Several threads want the same lock at overlapping times
A thread uses only private variables
A disk has unused free blocks
explanation: Contention causes waiting or retries because a resource has competing requesters.

questionText: x starts at 0. T1 loads x, T2 loads x, T1 stores its value+1, T2 stores its value+2. What is final x?
explanation: Both loads see 0; T1 stores 1, then T2 stores 2 from its stale value, so the final value is 2.

questionText: Why can pointer CAS succeed even after an object was removed and another object reused its address?
options: The address can change from A to B and back to A while identity changes
Memory addresses can never be reused
CAS always fails after the first allocation
CAS compares full object histories automatically
explanation: Comparing only the current bit pattern misses intervening changes; tagged versions or safe reclamation can address this ABA hazard.

questionText: A producer initializes data then sets ready using a release store. A consumer observes that store using an acquire load. What guarantee is intended?
options: Earlier producer writes become visible to the acquiring consumer
Data becomes durable against power loss
Acquire makes uninitialized data valid before release
Every unrelated future write becomes ordered automatically
explanation: A matching release/acquire synchronization publishes prior writes; the consumer must actually observe the relevant release sequence.

questionText: What does lock-free progress generally guarantee?
options: No thread can ever retry
Some operation completes despite contention, not that every thread finishes promptly
The algorithm never uses atomic instructions
Every individual thread has bounded completion time
explanation: Lock-free is a system-wide progress guarantee; wait-free is the stronger per-operation bounded-step guarantee under its model.

questionText: A protected section takes 2 ms per operation and cannot overlap. Ignoring other costs, what is its maximum service rate?
options: 2000 operations/s
500 operations/s
2 operations/s
50 operations/s
explanation: One second contains 1000 ms; 1000/2=500 serialized operations per second.

questionText: Why is double-checked initialization with an ordinary unsynchronized shared pointer unsafe in languages such as C++?
options: Constructors cannot allocate memory
A second check automatically creates acquire semantics
It can race and expose incompletely published state
Pointer assignment necessarily flushes persistent storage
explanation: Correct publication needs the language's synchronization guarantees; a lock on only one path does not make all accesses safe.

questionText: In a linked-list traversal using lock coupling, why acquire the next node's lock before releasing the current one?
options: To eliminate every possible ordering issue regardless of implementation
To ensure all nodes remain locked forever
To make deletion of any unlocked node impossible globally
To keep the traversed link/node relationship protected during movement
explanation: Overlapping lock ownership can stabilize traversal locally, provided insertion/deletion use a compatible protocol and ordering.

questionText: A queue becomes nonempty with one item while ten consumers wait. Why can broadcast cause unnecessary work?
options: Every consumer is guaranteed to remove a different item
The mutex disappears on broadcast
Broadcast gives each consumer a separate copy automatically
Many consumers may wake and contend although only one can consume the item
explanation: All awakened consumers recheck the predicate; all but one may need to wait again, causing a thundering herd.

questionText: A thread dies while holding a robust mutex. What must a recovering owner typically consider?
options: All writes by the dead thread are automatically rolled back
The mutex's memory contains a full transaction log by definition
Protected state may be inconsistent and require repair
The state is guaranteed correct merely because ownership changed
explanation: Owner-death notification enables recovery, but application-level invariants still need validation or reconstruction.

questionText: Why must a bounded-buffer producer wait for an empty slot before locking the buffer mutex, if consumers need that mutex to remove items?
options: Otherwise a full-buffer producer can hold the mutex while waiting for a consumer that needs it
A consumer never touches the buffer mutex
Semaphore waits cannot block inside locks
Mutex acquisition automatically increments the empty count
explanation: The wrong order can block the producer while excluding the very consumer that would create space.
